claim: balenaOS release analysed: meta-balena tag v9.0.6, commit 48184b6, committed 2026-11-09
balena Supervisor release analysed: v20.0.7, commit 321c7d3, committed 2026-11-09
meta-balena (the balenaOS build layer) is licensed Apache-2.0
The balena Supervisor is licensed Apache-2.0
balenaEngine is a Moby-based container engine licensed Apache-2.0 (GitHub license API; repo not archived, last push 2026-11-05)
openBalena (the self-hosted server) is licensed AGPL-3.0
openBalena is single-user, managed through balena-cli only, has no web dashboard, no binary delta updates and no remote diagnostics; these are balenaCloud-only
The balenaOS disk image has five partitions: boot (resin-boot), root A, root B, state (resin-state) and data (resin-data)
Default sizes: boot 100 MiB, state 80 MiB; each root slot is sized from a fixed 1460 MiB image budget minus boot and state, divided by two (~640 MiB per slot by default)
The root filesystem is built by Yocto, imported as a Docker image (docker import/save), then written with mkfs.hostapp into a hostapp-ext4 root partition: the OS itself is a container image

Image and EFI/RSA signing at build time is done by calling a remote signing service (SIGN_API with an API key header), so private keys are not on the build host; a signed build produces a balenaos-img.sig

The host OS update client (hostapp-update) pulls the new OS as a container image with balenaEngine (or loads a local tarball), creates it in the inactive sysroot and atomically switches the 'current' symlink there
Before updating, hostapp-update records whether the VPN (cloud link) was online, for the post-update health check
hostapp-update first deletes every container, image and hostapp in the inactive sysroot, so the previous-previous OS is gone before the new one is written
Docs: the updater tries a delta first, then a full pull from balenaCloud's registry, and falls back to Docker Hub if both fail
During an update the 80-rollback hook writes rollback-health and rollback-altboot breadcrumb files to the state partition
rollback-health waits 60 s after boot, then retries the health tests every 60 s up to 15 times; on failure it runs the previous OS's hooks from the inactive root and reboots into it
When tests pass, rollback-health commits: balena-extension-manager hup commit, rollback-stop, then commit hooks

The health tests check only (a) the VPN reconnects if it was online before the update, (b) the balenaEngine healthcheck and (c) an optional board-specific script; the Supervisor and user apps are not checked
rollback-altboot: the bootloader counts boots when upgrade_available=1 and boots the previous root if the count exceeds 1, i.e. the new OS never reached userspace
Docs: once a host OS update succeeds, there is no rollback to the previous OS version except the automatic rollbacks
Docs: since Q3 2026 OS updates are queued; the Supervisor fetches the request, retries twice, then every two days; offline devices update when they reconnect
The Supervisor refuses app updates and reboots while rollback breadcrumbs exist, so it cannot interrupt a host OS update on trial
On a UEFI device in Secure Boot user mode, the 0-signed-update hook aborts an update to an OS whose boot files are unsigned
The UEFI db is updated during the update, but the dbx (revocation list) update is deferred until rollback-health confirms the new OS
On TPM devices the update re-seals the disk-encryption passphrase to PCRs 0,2,3,7 including the new GRUB and kernel hashes
Docs: Secure Boot images are pre-signed with balena-owned keys (no Microsoft shim by default); customer keys are a paid extra service
Docs: the chain of trust ends at the kernel; the root filesystem is not signed or verified at runtime and integrity relies on disk encryption
Docs: application container images are not cryptographically signed; integrity relies on TLS to balenaCloud and digest-pinned pulls
Docs: Secure Boot and full-disk encryption are only offered together, through installer images; memory-constrained devices cannot support it
App format: a subset of Docker Compose v2.1; the Supervisor keeps an allow-list of compose fields and drops others with a warning
Per-service update strategy is a label (io.balena.update.strategy): download-then-kill (default), kill-then-download, delete-then-download, hand-over

Host access is granted by io.balena.features.* labels that the Supervisor turns into bind mounts or device requests (journal, dbus, kernel-modules, firmware, balena-socket, sysfs, procfs, gpu, supervisor-api)
Releases can declare contract requirements on sw.supervisor, sw.l4t, sw.os, hw.device-type and arch.sw; services can be marked optional
Device identity: a UUID plus a device API key; on first boot the Supervisor uses the fleet provisioning key from config.json to register the device key with balenaCloud
Docs: development mode exposes the container engine socket and passwordless root SSH and must never be used in production
Docs: offline updates are a reflash with a preloaded image that keeps the device identity; pre-provisioned named volumes are wiped
Docs: binary delta updates compare full images and download only the difference (balenaOS >= 2.47.1)
Docs: Extended Support Release (ESR) is a paid-plan feature; new ESR versions ship quarterly and each is supported for nine months with security and critical backports
Docs: the ESR device list includes generic-amd64, generic-aarch64 and raspberrypi5 but no Jetson Orin or Thor device type; other types need a request
balena-jetson-orin v8.0.0+ is based on L4T 39.2 / JetPack 7.2; moving from JetPack 6 requires first updating to L4T 36.5.0 (balenaOS v7.9.4)
balena-jetson-orin builds from OE4T meta-tegra (wrynose branch) rather than NVIDIA's Ubuntu rootfs
balena patches NVIDIA's UEFI (RootfsRetryCountMax 3→9) because in balenaOS the balena bootloader, not NVIDIA's rootfs A/B, picks the active root
Jetson board health check fails (forcing rollback) if the UEFI firmware's L4T version differs from the kernel's L4T version
Jetson host OS updates also stage a UEFI capsule (QSPI bootloader update) on the boot partition
Failure report: balenaOS 8.0.9 on AGX Orin 64GB with Kingston eMMC never cold-boots (MB2 eMMC init error) because the JP7.2 boot blob lacked NVIDIA's fix overlay
Failure report: a power cut during the first boot after an update caused an immediate rollback; retries were added in v2.85.10
Failure report: a failed host OS update did not roll back the Supervisor's config; a support engineer restored it by hand
Failure report: broken I2C on Raspberry Pi 5 (kernel 6.6.22) for a customer; balena replied it does not monitor GitHub issues and asked for paid support channels
On Raspberry Pi 5, balenaOS drops U-Boot and boots through the kexec-based balena bootloader (99-balena-bootloader hook)
The raspberrypi5 device type (Pi 5 and CM5) is in state 'released'

balenaCloud pricing: Free for 10 devices; Prototype $159/month (30 devices); Pilot $329/month (60); Production $1,439/month (110); extra devices $2–3/device/month; ESR on paid plans; ARM64 secure boot from Pilot up
Docs: Custom Device Support is a paid service (custom balenaOS build plus maintenance for a monthly fee)
balena (formerly resin.io) was founded in 2013 and announced a $14.4M round led by OpenView on 2019-07-24
meta-balena commit history 2025-11-10 to 2026-11-09: about 15 distinct human authors, top 5 make ~88% of human commits (bots excluded)

The only balena-owned device-control MCP server found is balena-io-experimental/balenamcp: a CLI wrapper, created 2025-05-23, last pushed 2025-05-26, archived
No on-device backup or restore feature is documented: 'backup' appears in no balenaOS reference or deploy page in the docs repo at 6b96293 (only device-debugging and getting-started pages)
Docs: balenaOS ships NetworkManager + ModemManager, Avahi mDNS, chrony, and OpenVPN to balenaCloud's cloudlink for remote access
Docs: the read-only root keeps persistent paths on resin-state via bind mounts; apps, the Supervisor and volumes live on resin-data
